segments: There's a phone on a coffee table, and
there's a man on a couch looking at it.
He's not going to pick it up.
He wants to - that's the whole thing.
He wants to call his friend.
Not make a friend;
he has one, a real one, twenty years
of history, a best man's toast, the
whole file.
He just wants to call the guy, and
somehow the phone weighs six hundred pounds.
Tomorrow morning he'll lift dumbbells
that weigh less than this phone.
This is the smallest want a man can
have, and he can't do it -
and most of us have sat on this couch.
Why not?
That's the question, and the answer
takes a hundred years of our history
to explain. Start with the sentence,
because you know the sentence - you've
said the sentence.
"We should hang out sometime."
We say it in parking lots, at
funerals, at the end of weddings, in
the cereal aisle.
And here's the thing about "we should
hang out sometime":
it has never once, in recorded
history, produced a hanging-out.
It's not a plan;
it's the opposite of a plan.
It's a little ceremony we perform so
we can both walk away, and we do walk away -
you've seen us do it.
The backward walk down the sidewalk,
waving, still talking, "yeah,
definitely, sometime,"
each step making it a little less true.
By the time your friend reaches his
car, "sometime" means never,
and you both know it, and neither of
you is lying, exactly. You mean it.
You just can't do it.
Now the numbers, because this isn't
one man on one couch - this is us.
In 1990, three percent of American men
said they had no close friends.
Not few; none.
By 2021 that was fifteen percent,
which means it quintupled.
And the men with ten or more close
friends, the guys with a whole bench,
went from forty percent down to fifteen.
Women declined too, but less - so this
isn't everybody's story equally;
something happened to the men specifically.
The Surgeon General reached for the
word "epidemic,"
and that's his word, not ours.
When a number quintuples, you don't
get to call it a personality problem;
something in our machinery broke.
What you're seeing on that couch isn't
a personality - it's a trend line,
sitting down.
And here's the machinery, up close -
here's why the phone weighs six
hundred pounds.
Say you're forty, and you want to
propose a friendship.
What are you going to say - "do you
want to be friends?" You can't say that;
that's a sentence for a seven-year-old
with a juice box,
and there's no adult version of it.
You can propose marriage - there's a ring,
a knee, a script, a whole apparatus.
You can propose a merger.
You can propose a toast.
But there is no ritual, anywhere in
our culture, for one grown man saying
to another grown man:
you, specifically, Tuesdays.
So we say "we should hang out
sometime," which is the ritual for not
saying it.
The want is enormous, and the
vocabulary is missing.
It wasn't always missing.
There are photographs in the Met - a
whole collection, more than a hundred
studio portraits from the
eighteen-forties through 1918 - of
American men posing together. Holding hands.
Arms wrapped around each other.
Sitting in each other's laps.
In a lap, at a photographer's studio,
on purpose, for money,
to mark the friendship.
And nobody blinked.
The historians who study these pictures
say the poses were common, unremarkable -
affection between men wasn't a
confession back then.
It was furniture.
These men paid a professional to
document how much they liked each other. Then
the twentieth century
taught us restraint instead,
and the lap became the handshake,
and the handshake became the nod, and
the nod became "we should hang out
sometime." Because that intimacy was
normal, the men who had it did a very
American thing
when the industrial cities started
pulling life apart:
they built infrastructure for it.
Look behind our man on the couch,
because his great-grandfather is
standing there, and his
great-grandfather is wearing a costume.
He belonged to a lodge - the Odd
Fellows, say, the largest order in the
country by 1900, three point three
million members at their 1920s peak.
At the height of what historians
actually call the Golden Age of Fraternalism,
roughly forty percent of adult
American men belonged to at least one order.
Forty percent - sit with that.
These men built marble temples on Main Street,
and inside them they had rituals,
degrees, regalia,
secret handshakes, a gavel.
They built an entire parallel
civilization, in costume,
and the stated product of the whole
operation was friendship.
That's what the dues bought.
The largest friendship machine ever
constructed, running on schedule, so
that no man would ever stand in a
parking lot inventing a reason to see
another man.
The reason was Tuesday.
The reason was always Tuesday.
And this is the fact that breaks our man.
His great-grandfather had a temple - a
temple, a costume, a title, and a
standing appointment - and forty
percent of men had some version of it.
He can't send a text.
The text is eleven words.
His ancestor memorized initiation
rites in a room full of columns, and
he's on a couch, defeated by "hey, you
around this week?" That's not evolution;
that's demolition.
You can even watch us do the
dismantling inside a single sport.
Between 1980 and 1993, the number of
American bowlers rose ten percent -
bowling was fine, bowling was up.
But league bowling - same lanes, same
shoes, same ball, plus other people
every week - fell forty percent.
We kept the hobby and fired the humans.
Nearly ten million Americans bowled in
leagues at the late-seventies peak;
by the 2022 season, barely a million
of us were left.
The pins are fine and the beer is fine.
The Tuesday-night guys who knew your
name and noticed when you didn't show
- that's the part we cancelled.
It's the lodge,
dying a second death in rented shoes.
Now put the jokes down, because
there's a bill.
In 2010, a researcher named Julianne
Holt-Lunstad pooled 148 studies -
three hundred thousand people followed
over time -
and measured what weak social
connection does to your odds of dying early.
The effect size was comparable to
smoking up to fifteen cigarettes a day.
Hear that precisely:
a comparable effect size, across
studies - not "loneliness is smoking."
That's the telephone-game version, and
the claim gets flattened almost every
time it's repeated;
the researcher herself keeps asking
people to stop.
The honest version is heavy enough.
As a risk factor, disconnection sits
in the same league as a serious
cigarette habit.
And there's a longer receipt.
Harvard has been following the same
men since 1938 - the longest study of
adult life ever run -
and one finding stands over the rest:
how satisfied people were with their
relationships at fifty predicted their
health at eighty
better than their cholesterol did -
better than cholesterol.
The study's director compresses it to
one line -
good relationships keep us happier and
healthier.
So the couch, the phone, the unsent text:
that isn't a social nicety our man is
neglecting.
That's a vital sign. So
what does the repair cost? It turns out
friendship has a posted price,
measured in hours.
A researcher named Jeffrey Hall ran
the numbers:
roughly fifty hours of contact to make
a casual friend,
about ninety for real friendship,
two hundred plus for a close one.
Two hundred hours sounds like a debt,
but it's a recipe,
because Hall found something better.
The hours aren't equal.
Hours spent joking around with no
agenda count far more than hours spent
working side by side.
Take that in slowly:
the useless hours are the valuable ones.
The hanging out is itself the mechanism.
Which is exactly what the lodge was selling.
Nobody needed the fez;
the fez was packaging.
The product was two hundred
agenda-less hours a year,
pre-scheduled, no proposal required.
The temple was never a mystery.
It was a payment plan.
Our great-grandfathers didn't have
better hearts than we do.
They had better calendars.
Back to the living room -
but pull back further this time,
because you've only seen half the picture.
Across town there's a second living
room: another couch, another lamp,
another phone lying face up on another
coffee table.
And leaning at that phone is the friend -
the very name glowing in the first
man's contacts.
He wants to make the same call.
He's wanted to for weeks, and he can't
do it either.
Two men, two rooms,
one silence -
and neither of them built it.
Nobody here is pathetic, and nothing
in either man is defective.
Jobs moved them, kids rearranged them,
the lodge closed, the league folded,
and the rule they both inherited said
men hold still.
The machinery of adult life did this -
to both of them at once -
which means the silence between them
is nobody's verdict on anybody.
Then one of them picks up the phone,
and it genuinely doesn't matter which.
He presses the name - that's the
entire heroic act,
one thumb, half an inch of travel.
And the last thing you see isn't his face.
It's the other living room, where a
dark screen suddenly lights up,
and a man moving faster than he's
moved in years nearly takes out the
coffee table getting to it.
Because that's the mercy hiding inside
all those numbers.
If fifteen percent of men have no one to call,
then in living rooms everywhere,
phones are lying face up next to men
who are waiting -
waiting for exactly the call you've
been assuming would bother them.
The line isn't engaged.
It was never engaged.
So the sentence gets one small renovation:
"we should hang out sometime" becomes
"Tuesday, the garage, seven o'clock."
Two lawn chairs, two sodas, no agenda,
and a clock quietly running toward two
hundred.
We don't need the temple back.
We don't need the robes, the degrees,
or, tragically, the hats.
All we ever needed was the thing the
temple was actually selling, and we
can afford it.
It was never about the lodge.
It was about Tuesday.
Pick a Tuesday.
